planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; maximum gold speckling in Gold Dust requires high light.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Gold Dust is a fine-textured croton with narrow, glossy, deep green leaves finely peppered in small golden-yellow flecks, a much subtler, more scattered variegation pattern than the bold, broad color bands of showier crotons like Petra, giving it a softer, more understated look useful for adding texture without overwhelming color to a mixed tropical planting. Bright light is essential for developing and holding the gold speckling; plants grown in low light gradually fade toward plain green. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance and drops leaves readily below 50°F.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Mrs. Iceton is a long-cultivated, classic croton with broad oval leaves speckled and splashed in pink, red, and yellow over a dark green background, an older heirloom-style croton pattern that predates flashier modern cultivars like Petra but remains popular for its rich rose and crimson tones. Bright light develops and holds the strongest pink-red speckling; plants in lower light fade toward plain green and lose much of their color interest. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance and drops leaves readily below 50°F.

Picasso's Paintbrush is a narrow-leaved croton with thin, twisting, brush-like leaves splashed in unpredictable streaks of red, orange, yellow, and green, as though each leaf had been dabbed with paint, giving it a wilder, more abstract look than the broad, symmetrically patterned leaves of Petra-type crotons. Its fine, airy texture works well as a textural contrast planted alongside bolder, broad-leaved crotons and other tropical foliage. Bright light develops and holds the strongest coloring; plants in lower light fade toward plain green. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance.

Banana croton carries long, narrow, gently curved leaves in shades of yellow and lime-green that mature to deeper green with age, resembling a bunch of small bananas hanging from the stem, giving the plant a distinctive fine, elongated texture unlike the broad or lobed leaves of most crotons. Its softer, more grassy-looking foliage works well as a textural filler among bolder broad-leaved tropicals. Bright light develops and holds the best yellow-green coloring; plants in lower light fade toward plain green. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance.

Zanzibar croton has very narrow, ribbon-like, gently twisting leaves striped and blushed in red, orange, and yellow over a green base, giving it an especially fine, willowy texture among crotons, most of which carry broader oval or lobed leaves. The slender, cascading foliage moves easily in a breeze, adding movement to a mixed tropical planting or container arrangement in a way that broader-leaved crotons cannot match. Bright light develops and holds the strongest coloring; plants in lower light fade toward plain green. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance.

common_name: Eleanor Roosevelt Croton (Narrow Curly Multi-Color Croton)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; maximum color intensity requires high light.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Eleanor Roosevelt is an heirloom croton cultivar with narrow, twisted, curling leaves marked in an unpredictable mix of red, orange, yellow, pink, and green, giving each plant a shaggy, wild, multicolored texture distinct from the broad, flatter leaves of more formal croton cultivars. Its curled, corkscrewing leaf form has made it a long-time favorite among croton collectors for the way individual leaves seem to twist in different directions across the plant. Bright light develops and holds the strongest, most varied coloring; plants in lower light fade toward plain green. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance.
